sections.body_en:
Three who ate bread together are obligated to make a zimun, that is, to add an introductory blessing to Birkat Ha-mazon. And if ten ate together, an additional distinction is added for them, in that they mention God's name in the zimun (below, halakha 5).1

To expand a little on the meaning of zimun, it must be explained that a gathering of many has great power; the mutual enrichment between them creates something additional, more than what each of the individuals has. The smallest group numbers three people, and when three people eat together, beyond the benefit and enjoyment they derive from the food, additional feelings are aroused in their souls; their meal takes on the status of a social event, and correspondingly their Birkat Ha-mazon too must take on a more important status. This is the purpose of zimun, for the distinction of Birkat Ha-mazon recited with a zimun is greater than its distinction without a zimun, since through three uniting to bless together, God's name is sanctified and the honor of Heaven increases. And so it is stated (Tehillim 34:4): "Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt His name together." Thus there is a distinction in one inviting his companions to exalt and magnify God's name together with him. And so it is stated (Devarim 32:3): "When I call upon the name of the Lord, ascribe greatness to our God" (Berakhot 45a).

There are spiritual outlooks in the world according to which eating is a contemptible necessity that one should be ashamed of, and it is fitting for a person to eat alone in order to hide his disgrace. In their view, the social custom of gathering to eat together is a contemptible and ugly custom, which grants ritual importance to the body and its desires, and destroys a person's ability to detach himself somewhat from the shackles of physicality. But according to the Torah outlook, the body is bad only when it is detached from values; but when the aim of eating is to receive strength, vitality and joy, for a good life of values, then eating is good.

However, one must be diligent about this, for just as it is possible to elevate the aim of eating, so the desire for eating can drag a person after it, make him forget his destiny and debase his life. This is the purpose of the blessings – to remind a person of the One to whom the food belongs, and consequently of the place and role of man in the world.

When a person eats in company, the meal is accompanied by many more emotions. And so we find that a good meal intensifies feelings of friendship between friends and family members, and can even create closeness between people who are distant. In contrast, a bad and tense meal can arouse negative feelings and intensify quarrels. And since a group meal carries greater weight, the regular blessings that suffice to elevate the meal of an individual do not suffice for a group, and therefore the group must enhance Birkat Ha-mazon through the blessing of the zimun.

It is worth adding that the feeling of social cohesion created at a meal may serve as a substitute for holy values, and thereby cause an overemphasis on the material side of life. Therefore, three who eat together must say words of Torah. As Rabbi Shimon said (Avot 3:3): "Three who ate at one table and did not say words of Torah over it, it is as if they ate of sacrifices to the dead, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 28:8): 'For all tables are full of vomit and filth, without place.' But three who ate at one table and said words of Torah over it, it is as if they ate from the table of the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is stated (Yeḥezkel 41:22): 'And he said to me, This is the table that is before the Lord.'"

notes_en.en: According to nearly all the Rishonim, zimun is rabbinic, and this is the view of Rav Natronai Gaon, the Rid, the Ra'ah, the Rashba, the Meiri and many others. So too wrote most of the Aḥaronim, among them the Ḥayei Adam and MB 192:1. According to the Ra'avad, the mitzva of zimun is from the Torah, and some say that zimun with ten is from the Torah and with three is rabbinic (Mabit).

sections.title_en: The Mitzva of Zimun When They Ate Together
sections.body_en:
When are the diners obligated to make a zimun? When they established themselves to eat together, for example, if they said to one another, "Let us eat together," or "Let us eat in a certain place." And even if they did not say anything to one another, but it is clear to them that they are eating together, such as family members eating dinner together, or good friends eating together, they are like those who established themselves to eat together, and they are obligated to make a zimun. The sign that they established themselves to eat together is that if one of them decided to leave in the middle of the meal without a special reason, it would be considered impolite, for they established themselves to eat together, so how can he withdraw from the group?

Even if only two began the meal, if afterward another person joined them to eat with them together, with the intention of staying with them until the end of the meal, they have become obligated in zimun.

There is an intermediate situation in which there is a mitzva to make a zimun but no obligation: when there is a connection between the diners, in that they are eating together and talking a little with one another, but they did not establish themselves to eat together, and if one of them withdrew in the middle it would not appear impolite. In this situation they are not obligated to make a zimun, but if they do make a zimun they fulfill a mitzva. And when there is no connection at all between the diners, as for example in a restaurant, when they sit at separate tables, they do not join together for a zimun.

In a yeshiva, or in a public institution, where everyone comes to eat at a fixed time in the dining room: if there were friends there who made a point of eating together at one table, to the extent that it would be impolite for one of them to leave before his friends, they are obligated to make a zimun. And those who do not make a point of sitting specifically with certain friends and beginning the meal together, and if one of them withdrew before his friends it would not be considered impolite, are in an intermediate situation – they are not obligated to make a zimun, but if they do they fulfill a mitzva. And if they are always accustomed to make a zimun, their custom of making a zimun creates a certain togetherness between them, and it is reasonable to say that they are obligated to make a zimun. But one who from the outset wanted to hurry without being dependent on his tablemates, since he made up his mind that he is not joining in fellowship with them, may recite Birkat Ha-mazon without a zimun.

All this concerns those sitting at one table, but people at separate tables do not join together for a zimun, because there is no connection between them. However, where people at adjacent tables talk with one another, they are permitted to join together for a zimun.

At a Shabbat meal, where all the diners are accustomed to sing together and hear words of Torah together, even though they sit at separate tables, they all join together. And if there were ten, they are obligated in a zimun of ten. Likewise at a brit mila meal, sheva berakhot, a wedding and the like, since everyone came to participate in the same event, they are all considered as eating together. And although at each table there are fewer than ten, since together they are more than ten, they are all obligated in a zimun of ten (see below, 11).

Those who eat while traveling in a vehicle: if they are traveling together and eating together, they are obligated to make a zimun. If each one eats for himself and it merely happened that they ate at the same time, they should not make a zimun. And if some connection was formed between them, it is a mitzva that they make a zimun, but not an obligation (see SA 193:3).2

notes_en.en:
The main thing depends on their gathering together in fellowship (so wrote the Behag, the Semag and the Riva, as cited in BY 193:2-3; the Ra'ah and the Ritva on Berakhot 42; Or Zaru'a 1:150). It seems that all the disputes on this matter revolve around a single axis: whether or not there is a gathering in fellowship here (and not as several books of our time have made the law depend on external definitions). We will detail the central disputes: 1) According to Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, only if they began the meal together did they become obligated in zimun, and according to the Rosh and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, even if they finished together they became obligated in zimun, and so wrote SA 193:2. 2) If they began together and do not want to finish together, according to the Baḥ and the Magen Avraham they are not obligated in zimun, while according to SA 200:1 and most poskim, among them the Taz, the Ma'amar Mordekhai, the Eliya Rabba and MB 200:5, since they began together they are obligated in zimun. 3) If two began, and afterward a third joined, and one of them wants to leave before the other two have finished: according to most poskim, among them the Taz, the Ma'amar Mordekhai, the Ḥayei Adam and MB 193:19, they are not obligated to make a zimun, because the fact that they do not intend to finish together proves that they did not gather together for the meal in fellowship. According to the Eliya Rabba and the Nehar Shalom, even if they established themselves to sit together in the middle of the meal without beginning and finishing together, they became obligated (and so wrote Arukh Ha-shulḥan 193:15 and Maharil Diskin, Kuntres Aḥaron 5:20). However, it seems that even most poskim would agree that if the third person who joined intended to stay until the end and suddenly had to leave, since they intended to gather together in fellowship, even though they did not begin or finish together, they are obligated in zimun. And all that they wrote, that the end of the meal is determinative, refers to a situation in which they did not agree to eat together. 4) They further disagreed about a situation in which there is no obligation to make a zimun: according to the Rema 193:2 and most poskim (Levush, Baḥ, Perisha, Eliya Rabba, Magen Giborim, Taz 195:1, Arukh Ha-shulḥan 193:12, Kaf Ha-ḥayim 16), they are permitted, and it is even a mitzva, to make a zimun. According to the Magen Avraham 193:8 and those who share his view, as long as they have not become obligated in zimun, they are not permitted to make a zimun, and MB 24 inclines toward this. However, where there is a doubt whether they are obligated in zimun, it is proper that they make a zimun (Eliya Rabba 193:7). So too wrote the Ḥayei Adam and MB 193:26, that in a case of doubtful obligation they should make a zimun, but if they are ten, because of the doubt they should not mention God's name.
In summary, this is the rule: 1) If they established themselves to eat together, to the extent that the departure of one of them in the middle would be considered impolite, they are obligated to make a zimun, and a sign of this is that they began the meal together or intended to finish it together. 2) If there is a certain connection between those sitting, without a commitment to stay together until the end, they are permitted to make a zimun if they wish, but they are not obligated; and this is the law for yeshiva students sitting around one table. This is because according to most poskim the halakha follows the Rema, that there is an intermediate situation in which they are permitted to make a zimun even though they are not obligated. In addition, it is possible that even according to the Magen Avraham, through their wish to make a zimun they became people eating together in fellowship and became obligated in it, and all the more so when they are accustomed to make a zimun. 3) If there is no connection at all between them, they should not make a zimun, for the foundation of zimun depends on togetherness, and when there is no connection at all between the diners there is no zimun. This is the law for people at different tables in a restaurant, and people at different tables in a yeshiva: since there is no connection between them, they do not make a zimun together.

sections.title_en: Not Breaking Up a Zimun Group and Not Leaving It
sections.body_en:
If two were eating together and they have the opportunity to invite another person to eat with them, it is a mitzva to invite him, so that they will be able to bless with a zimun (SA 193:1; MB 7. See halakha 10 regarding with which food and drink the third person joins the zimun).

Since there is a mitzva to make a zimun, it is forbidden for three, four or five who have become obligated in zimun to split up, for if they split up they will lose the zimun and diminish the honor of Heaven. Only if there were six there may they split into two groups of three, each of which makes a zimun separately. Likewise, it is forbidden for ten who ate together to split up, so that they will not lose the mention of God's name. And if there were twenty, they may split into two groups, in both of which they will mention God's name (Berakhot 50a; SA 193:1).

Three who ate bread together, and mistakenly blessed without making a zimun, have lost the mitzva of zimun. Even if only two of them mistakenly blessed without making a zimun, they have lost the zimun. But if only one of them mistakenly blessed, although he has lost his mitzva, since two remain who are still obligated in zimun, the two may make a zimun with him, for since he ate with them, he can answer "Blessed is He of whose food we have eaten" and join the zimun (SA 194:1).3

Three who ate together, and two of them have finished their meal and want to make a zimun and bless: the one who wants to continue eating must stop and join them for the zimun, and afterward continue eating, and when he finishes he should recite Birkat Ha-mazon by himself. And although ideally it is a mitzva that the zimun be adjacent to Birkat Ha-mazon, for then it serves as a preparation for the blessing, and if he joins them he will be forced to recite Birkat Ha-mazon separately from the zimun; since he fulfills the mitzva of zimun even when the zimun is not adjacent to Birkat Ha-mazon, he must defer to the majority and join the zimun. And if he insists on not joining them, they can nevertheless make a zimun including him, and if he does not respond, he loses his mitzva, but the two fulfill the mitzva, for since the third was there at the time of the zimun, he joins them against his will to make three.

And if one wants to finish his meal and withdraw from the group, and the two want to continue their meal, the individual cannot compel his companions to make a zimun before they finish the meal, and he must stay until they finish their meal and make a zimun and bless together. And this is the rule – we always follow the majority: if the diners were five, we follow the three. Likewise, if there were more than ten, the majority determines whether to bless or to continue the meal (SA 200:1).

And if the individual who wants to make a zimun is the father or the rabbi of the diners, they are obligated to honor him and join him for the zimun (Birkei Yosef 200:2).

Although we have learned that the two are not obligated to take into account the individual who wants to finish his meal and make a zimun, it is a custom of piety that they take him into account and join him for the zimun, and afterward continue their meal. But if there is a certain impudence in his leaving before the end of the meal, they need not take him into account, and he must stay with them until the end of the meal in order to bless with a zimun. And if the two have already finished their meal, even though they thought to linger longer, they may not delay the individual any further, and they must join him for the zimun (BHL 200:1, s.v. "ad." See halakha 11 regarding in which situations a person is permitted to bless without a zimun).4

notes_en.en:
Likewise in a zimun of ten, if three blessed, the remaining seven may join them to the zimun with the mention of God's name (BHL 194:1, s.v. "eḥad." And see halakha 10, that one who ate mezonot and blessed does not join).
Three who ate together, and one of them went out to the market: when his companions want to bless, they should call him, so that he will join them for the zimun. And even if he is not sitting with them, but only stands opposite the doorway and shows himself to them and hears them, he joins the zimun with them. All this applies to a zimun of three, but for a zimun of ten, since they must mention God's name, out of respect for the mention of God's name one should not include someone who is not sitting with them (SA 194:2).

It should be added that interrupting in the middle of the meal for a zimun is only after the fact (be-di'avad), not only because it is proper to attach the zimun to Birkat Ha-mazon, but also because according to several Rishonim, among them Rav Hai Gaon and the Ra'avad, after interrupting for a zimun, if they want to continue the meal they must wash their hands and recite Ha-motzi. And although in practice SA 200:1 ruled in accordance with the view of the Behag, the Rosh and Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona that they should continue eating without a blessing, ideally it is preferable not to enter into this doubt.

sections.title_en: Who Is Fit to Lead the Zimun
sections.body_en:
It is a great mitzva to be the one who leads the zimun (the mezamen). And so it is related in the Talmud (Berakhot 53b) that Rav Huna said to his son: if they honor you with leading the zimun over the cup, seize the mitzva and bless. A guest in particular must be careful that if he is honored with leading the zimun over a cup of wine, he not refuse, since within his blessing he must include a blessing for the host, and if he refuses, he is refusing to bless the host. The Sages said (Berakhot 55a) that one who refuses to bless over the cup of blessing causes his days and years to be shortened. And even when the zimun is without a cup of wine, it is of great importance, and one should seek it out, and it is fitting for a guest not to refuse to lead the zimun (SA 201:3). However, on the other hand, it is forbidden for a person to pursue honor, and therefore if his companions do not honor him with leading the zimun, he should not push himself to lead the zimun against his companions' wishes.

When there is a Torah scholar among the diners, it is a mitzva to honor him with the zimun. Likewise, if there is a kohen there, it is a mitzva to honor him with the zimun, for the Sages learned (Gittin 59b) from what is stated (Vayikra 21:8), "You shall sanctify him," that it is a mitzva to give the kohen precedence in every matter of holiness (Magen Avraham 201:4). And if there were a Torah scholar and a kohen who is not a Torah scholar there, the Torah scholar takes precedence. And it is forbidden for a Torah scholar to lower himself before the kohen, because the honor of the Torah takes precedence over the honor of the priesthood (Megilla 28a).

But if it is clear that the honor belongs to the Torah scholar, the Torah scholar may give the kohen permission to lead the zimun. And even when the kohen is a Torah scholar but the Yisrael is a greater Torah scholar, the distinction of the one greater in Torah takes precedence; but in such a case, it is a measure of piety that the one greater in Torah honor the kohen with leading the zimun (Tosafot there; Rema 167:14; MB 71). Likewise, a sage may say that another person should be honored with the zimun, in order to educate and encourage him (SA 201:1-2).

The Sages further said (Sota 38b): "The cup of blessing is given to bless only to one who has a good eye," that is, to one who hates ill-gotten gain and does kindness with his money (Rashi). For since he is not envious and rejoices in the good of others, he will direct his intent more toward good in Birkat Ha-mazon, and especially in the guest's blessing. And presumably a Torah scholar also has a good eye.

When the diners are guests of the host, it is customary to let one of the guests lead the zimun, even when the host is the wisest among them. This is because in the past, the mezamen was the only one who blessed aloud, and the other diners would intend to fulfill their obligation through his blessing, and when the guest blessed, he would add the "guest's blessing" (birkat ha-oreaḥ) to his blessing (above 4:2). Even today, when each person blesses for himself, there is reason to let the guest lead the zimun, so that he will say the guest's blessing aloud as part of Birkat Ha-mazon, and the other diners will answer "Amen" after him. However, if the host wishes, it is his right to take the mitzva of zimun for himself, and so several great authorities were accustomed to do. But if one of the guests is a Torah scholar and the host is not a Torah scholar, it is proper that he honor the Torah scholar with the zimun. In any case, even when the guest does not lead the zimun, it is good that he say the guest's blessing aloud, so that the other diners will answer "Amen" after him.

It should be noted that many guests of Ashkenazic descent are accustomed to make do with a short blessing: "May the Merciful One bless the master of this house." Many have wondered at this: why do they not say the wording of the detailed blessing that the Sages instituted (Leḥem Ḥamudot; MB 201:5, as cited above 4:2)? It is more correct that guests of Ashkenazic descent too say the wording of the guest's blessing, and it is fitting for this purpose to print the wording of the guest's blessing in all bentchers (birkonim).5

notes_en.en:
In Berakhot 46b it is related that Rabbi honored Rav, when he was young, with the blessing of the zimun, even though Rabbi Ḥiya, who was greater than him, was there. Most poskim learned from this that the host has the right to honor whichever guest he wishes, even if he is less of a Torah scholar than the other guest; so wrote the Rema 201:1, the Pri Megadim and the Ma'amar Mordekhai; see MB 4. SA 201:1 wrote that the host may honor himself with the zimun. And it is said in the Zohar that one honors with the zimun the person who said words of Torah (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 9). Further regarding the value of the cup of blessing, we learned in Ḥullin 87a that it is worth forty gold coins, for the mezamen recites four blessings over it and discharges the other listeners (and see halakha 6). Also at the time of the guest's blessing, the mezamen must raise the cup (Sha'arei Teshuva, end of 190).
Some say that what was said (Berakhot 55a), that a guest who refuses to lead the zimun shortens his days, refers specifically to a cup of wine (Magen Avraham 5). But the SA (201:3) did not mention a cup of wine. And some say that where in any case the mezamen does not say the guest's blessing, but rather everyone says "Ha-raḥaman" (as some of those of Ashkenazic descent are accustomed), there is no strictness about this (see Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 14). However, it can be said that the zimun itself is also a great thing, and therefore refusing to lead the zimun in His honor, may He be blessed, is in itself serious (see MB 14; Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 16; Ben Ish Ḥai, Shelaḥ 24). One who pays for his meal is not obligated to recite the guest's blessing (MB 201:7). The one who owns the meal is the host, and not the owner of the house (MB 201:3); however, it seems that if there is no one whose meal it is, the owner of the house is considered the host (so it is implied in Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 201:6).
The Tur learned from the Yerushalmi that a Levi should be given precedence over a Yisrael, while according to the Maharam of Rothenburg and most poskim there is no need to give precedence, and several Aḥaronim wrote that it is good to give precedence (MB 13, based on the Eliya Rabba and Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav). Some are accustomed to honor a mourner within twelve months with the zimun, just as they honor him with being the prayer leader, so that this will be an elevation of the soul of the deceased (MB 201:1; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 2).

sections.body_en:
The mitzva of zimun is as follows: the mezamen turns to his companions and says: "Let us bless the One of whose food we have eaten." And they answer after him: "Blessed is He of whose food we have eaten and through whose goodness we live." And he too says after them: "Blessed is He of whose food we have eaten and through whose goodness we live." And from this they begin Birkat Ha-mazon.

It is customary that before the main part of the zimun, the mezamen calls on the diners to participate in the blessing with the words "Hav lan ve-nevarekh" ("Give us [the cup] and let us bless") or "Rabbotai nevarekh" ("Gentlemen, let us bless"). And since the Sages did not fix a wording for this, there are differences between the customs in this matter (MB 192:2; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 2).6

When ten eat together, the Shekhina rests among them, for whenever ten Jews gather for a good purpose, the Shekhina rests among them; therefore they mention God's name in the zimun. The mezamen says: "Let us bless our God, of whose food we have eaten," and they answer: "Blessed is our God, of whose food we have eaten and through whose goodness we live." And he too answers after them: "Blessed is our God, of whose food we have eaten and through whose goodness we live." If the mezamen and the diners forgot to mention God's name, they have fulfilled the zimun but have lost the mention of God's name (SA 192:1-2).

Many are meticulous to raise themselves a little when God's name is mentioned, but this is not an obligation.7

One who did not eat and heard the mezamen say "Let us bless the One of whose food we have eaten" answers after him: "Blessed and praised be His name continually, forever and ever," for it is not fitting that a person hear his companions making a zimun while he stands aside without participating with them in praise of God. And if the zimun was with ten, he says: "Blessed is our God, and praised be His name continually, forever and ever." And if he did not hear the mezamen calling the diners to bless, but only heard the diners answering, "Blessed is He of whose food we have eaten and through whose goodness we live," he should answer "Amen" after them (SA 198:1). And he should also answer "Amen" again after the mezamen, who repeats their words (MB 198:4). For the zimun is considered a blessing, and whoever hears a blessing from his fellow must answer "Amen" after him. However, those who answer "Blessed and praised" etc. do not answer "Amen" after their companions and after the mezamen, because they are participants in the blessing itself.

One who ate a kezayit or drank a revi'it and has not yet recited the after-blessing, even though he did not eat with them, answers the entire wording, for he too can say "of whose food we have eaten" (MB 198:1).

notes_en.en:
The Aḥaronim wrote, based on the Zohar (vol. 3, 186b), that one must add an introduction to the zimun, in which the mezamen calls on the diners to participate in the blessing of the zimun. According to the custom of many of those of Sephardic descent, the mezamen says: "Hav lan ve-nivrikh le-malka ila'a kadisha" ("Give us [the cup] and let us bless the supreme holy King"). And they answer: "Shamayim" ("Heaven"), meaning, with the permission of Heaven. And again the mezamen says: "With the permission of the supreme holy King (and on Shabbat he adds: and with the permission of the Shabbat Queen), let us bless the One of whose food we have eaten." Those of Ashkenazic descent used to call the diners in Yiddish, and today many open in Hebrew: "Rabbotai nevarekh" ("Gentlemen, let us bless"). And the diners answer: "May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever." And the mezamen repeats and says: "May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever. With the permission of the gentlemen present, let us bless the One of whose food we have eaten."
When his father is present, he should say: "With the permission of my father, my teacher, and the gentlemen present," and in the presence of the rabbi he should begin with "With the permission of the rabbi," and if there is a kohen there he should add "With the permission of the kohen" or "the kohanim," and if he is a guest, he should add "With the permission of the master of the house" (SA 192:1; MB 192:2; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 2).
Some Ashkenazim are accustomed that after the mezamen finishes "and through whose goodness we live," he adds and says, "Blessed is He and blessed is His name," in order to distinguish between the zimun and the beginning of the blessing (Darkhei Moshe), and in order to add further praise for those answering (Maharal and Perisha). But the custom of Sephardim and of many Ashkenazim is not to say this addition, which is not mentioned in the Gemara or the Rishonim (Darkhei Moshe 192:2; MB 4; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 8).

My teacher and master, Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook ztz"l, was meticulous to stand at his full height at the mention of God's name in the zimun. But according to the law there is no need to raise oneself even a little (Eshel Avraham of Buczacz 192; Ḥatam Sofer OḤ 51).
If the mezamen forgot to mention God's name and remembered his error before the diners answered after him, he may go back and correct himself (SA 192:2). If he did not remember until the diners answered, and the diners remembered to say God's name, when the mezamen repeats their words he should mention God's name (MB 192:10). The Aḥaronim disagree about a situation in which the mezamen and the diners erred and did not mention God's name, and afterward the mezamen remembered: should he mention God's name when he repeats after them (MB 192:10)? "Sit and do not act" is preferable.

sections.title_en: The Mezamen and the Diners in Birkat Ha-mazon
sections.body_en:
In the days of the Sages, the practice was that the mezamen would recite Birkat Ha-mazon aloud, and the diners would direct their hearts to his blessing, answer "Amen" after him, and fulfill the obligation of Birkat Ha-mazon by listening. Ideally, this is preferable, for when everyone fulfills the blessing together, the honor of Heaven increases. However, the Rishonim wrote that since many find it difficult to concentrate on what the one blessing says, it is preferable that each of the diners say all of Birkat Ha-mazon with his own mouth together with the mezamen, for in this way they will concentrate more on the blessing (SA 183:7; MB 27). And since in any case the mezamen does not discharge the diners' obligation, many prefer that each person recite Birkat Ha-mazon for himself at the pace that suits him. Nevertheless, there is an enhancement of the mitzva in the mezamen reciting all the blessings in a loud voice and the diners saying Birkat Ha-mazon with him word for word, for in this way they have the distinction of "In the multitude of people is the King's glory." Furthermore, in this manner people generally concentrate more.8

The poskim disagree about how far the mitzva of zimun extends, that is, up to what point the diners must hear the mezamen in order to fulfill the obligation of zimun. Some say that the blessing of the zimun ends with saying "Blessed is He of whose food we have eaten and through whose goodness we live." Consequently, according to this view, although it is good that the diners hear the blessing of Ha-zan from the mezamen and say it with him quietly, in any case, even if they did not hear the blessing from him, they have fulfilled the mitzva of zimun. And one who interrupted in the middle of his meal to join the zimun may continue eating immediately after answering "Blessed is He of whose food we have eaten and through whose goodness we live." This is the custom of those of Sephardic descent (Rif, Rambam, and SA 200:2).

And some say that the mitzva of zimun continues until the end of the blessing of Ha-zan. So ruled the Ashkenazic poskim. According to this view, the mezamen must say the first blessing aloud, and the participants in the zimun must recite it quietly together with the mezamen. And especially those who join the zimun in the middle of their meal must stop eating and listen to the mezamen until the end of the blessing of Ha-zan. And if the mezamen did not say the blessing of Ha-zan aloud, they have not fulfilled the mitzva of zimun (Tosafot; Rosh; Rema; MB 183:28; Ben Ish Ḥai, Koraḥ 9).

In practice, ideally one should be careful to hear the entire blessing of Ha-zan from the mezamen, and when there are many diners, the mezamen should have a strong voice so that all the diners will hear him. After the fact, if the mezamen said the first blessing quietly, they have fulfilled the obligation of zimun.9

When the meal has many participants and it is difficult for the mezamen to make his voice heard without a loudspeaker, it is preferable that he use one, so that everyone will hear him and join in Birkat Ha-mazon, and the honor of Heaven will thereby increase. Even so, he should lead the zimun in a loud voice as far as he is able, so that as many people as possible will be able to hear his voice without the loudspeaker.10

notes_en.en:
So wrote BY 183:7, based on the Shibbolei Ha-leket, the Orḥot Ḥayim and the Tashbetz (and based on the Rosh regarding the blessings of Shema), that each person must bless quietly together with the mezamen. The Baḥ indeed disagreed with him, holding that the essence of the blessing of the zimun is that the mezamen discharge the listeners' obligation. However, most Aḥaronim wrote in accordance with the SA, that the mezamen should bless aloud and the diners should say the blessing with him word for word; so wrote Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 183:10, Ḥayei Adam 48:1 and MB 183:27. Only when someone is present who does not know how to bless does he fulfill his obligation by listening to the mezamen.
According to the Ashkenazic custom, it is proper that the diners be slightly ahead at the end of each blessing so that they can answer "Amen" after the mezamen (Rema 183:7). According to the Sephardic custom, they should not answer "Amen" after him, because as long as they are blessing themselves, they may not interrupt to answer "Amen"; therefore it is good that they finish the blessing together with the mezamen, so that they will not have the opportunity to answer "Amen" after him (Yabia Omer vol. 1, OḤ 11:6).

There is a dispute in Berakhot 46a: "Until where does the blessing of the zimun extend? Rav Naḥman said: until 'Nevarekh'; Rav Sheshet said: until 'Ha-zan.'" The Rif and the Rambam ruled in accordance with Rav Naḥman, and therefore the blessing of Ha-zan is not part of the zimun. According to the Behag, Tosafot, the Rosh and the Ra'avad, the halakha follows Rav Sheshet. However, they disagree in explaining his view: according to Tosafot, the Rosh and Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, only one who joins the zimun and intends to continue eating must hear Ha-zan, for since he is not blessing, the zimun has nothing to take effect upon if he does not hear until the end of Ha-zan; and so wrote the Rema 200:2. According to Rashi, Rabbeinu Ḥananel, the Ra'avad and the Tashbetz, according to Rav Sheshet the blessing of Ha-zan is part of the zimun, and whoever did not hear the blessing of Ha-zan from the mezamen, even if he said it himself, has not fulfilled the mitzva of zimun. So too wrote MB 183:28, that everyone must hear the mezamen say the blessing of Ha-zan and say it with him quietly word for word, and consequently one must be careful that the mezamen's voice be strong (MB 193:17). However, three who join ten so that they can mention God's name, and who intend afterward to make a zimun themselves (as below, 12), need not hear the blessing of Ha-zan from the mezamen, even according to the MB (MB 200:9).

See below 12:9, that the Aḥaronim disagree whether one can fulfill one's obligation by hearing through a loudspeaker. Regarding zimun there is an additional reason to be lenient (cited in Shevet Ha-Levi 10:40), for the zimun is meant to arouse the diners to sanctify God's name together in Birkat Ha-mazon, and it does not discharge them from the obligation of a blessing in which they are obligated; therefore it is not necessary that specifically the original voice of the mezamen be heard. However, some hold that zimun too is forbidden through a loudspeaker (see Piskei Teshuvot 193:3). According to their view, when there is no one there who can make his voice heard to everyone, it is preferable that they divide into groups of ten. However, in practice it seems that it is preferable to make the zimun with a loudspeaker, because the reasoning of the lenient view regarding zimun seems correct, and this is the prevalent custom, and through this the honor of Heaven increases. Furthermore, there is reason for concern that if they divide into groups, many will lose the zimun. However, ideally, in order to take into account the view of the stringent authorities, it is good that the mezamen raise his voice as far as he is able and hold the microphone a little away from his mouth, so that as many as possible will be able to hear him even had he not used the loudspeaker.

sections.body_en:
Women do not join with men for a zimun: if there were two men and a woman there, she does not join with them to create an obligation of zimun. The reason for this is modesty, for the zimun is created by eating together in the bond of companionship, since the power of a meal to bring distant people close to one another is great, and it is not fitting that there be a bond of companionship between men and women. Therefore the Sages did not institute a zimun for men and women together, and they did not distinguish in this between closer and less close relatives; therefore even a father with his daughter and son-in-law do not join together for a zimun.

But if there were three men there, since an obligation of zimun has already been created by the three men, the women sitting at the meal are also obligated to respond to the zimun. And there is no flaw of modesty in this, because the women are not partners with the men in creating the obligation, but rather join in responding to the zimun. One must be diligent in observing this halakha, for many times, when three men and some women eat at a family meal, although the women are obligated in the zimun, people forget to make sure that all the women participate in the zimun.11

Three women who ate together – the Sages did not impose upon them an obligation to make a zimun. This is because many women did not know Birkat Ha-mazon well, and some of them would make do with a short blessing in their own language instead of reciting the wording of Birkat Ha-mazon; therefore the Sages did not want to establish zimun for them as an additional obligation. Nevertheless, when three women sit together to eat, it is a mitzva that they bless with a zimun. There is only one difference in the law for women: even if there were ten, they do not make a zimun with the mention of God's name, because the mention of God's name is based on the law of a minyan, and the Sages did not institute the law of a minyan for women (SA 199:6-7).

And although in practice many women have not been accustomed to make a zimun, it is proper to encourage women to make a zimun. And even if there are one or two men there, they need not refrain from making a zimun. The men who are present must answer after the woman leading the zimun. If they ate a kezayit or drank a revi'it, they should answer according to the wording of the zimun; and if not, they should answer: "Blessed and praised be His name continually, forever and ever" (see halakha 5).12

notes_en.en:
When the woman is busy preparing and serving the food, and sometimes in the course of this also caring for the children, it can be said that she does not become obligated in the zimun, because she is not considered as sitting with them, as written in Igrot Moshe vol. 5, 9:10. But on Shabbat, and likewise a woman who sits with them and is not busy, one should be careful that she respond to the zimun.
Women who participated in a meal with three men and became obligated in zimun may, if they wish, make a zimun for themselves and leave before the men finish (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav; MB 18). But if they participated in a meal of ten, they cannot make a zimun for themselves, because they have already become obligated in a zimun with the mention of God's name (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 199:6). After the fact, when they need to leave, their law is like that of men (below 11, note 18): in a pressing situation they may bless without a zimun, and when possible they should make a zimun for themselves with three.

In the Mishna (Berakhot 45a) it is explained that women do not join with men for a zimun. But three women who ate by themselves are obligated to make a zimun according to Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, the Rosh and the Gra, and this is the meaning of the Gemara (45b): "Women make a zimun for themselves." And so it is explained in Arakhin 3a: "All are obligated in zimun," and the Gemara explained that this comes to include women. This is also the view of the Rambam (Hilkhot Berakhot 5:7, according to the precise version of the text).
In contrast, Tosafot there wrote that this is an optional mitzva for women, and it is possible that the Sages did not want to be stringent with women, since many of them did not properly know even Birkat Ha-mazon. And since it is an optional mitzva, women have not been accustomed to make a zimun, and only when there are three men at the meal are the women obligated to respond to their zimun, and this is what is discussed in Arakhin. So wrote Rashi and the Semag, and so it was ruled in SA 199:6-7. Another reason was mentioned for the mitzva being optional: because its essence is over a cup of wine, and for a woman who is not accustomed to this, drinking a cup of wine is unseemly (Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 6). In practice, women should be encouraged to fulfill the mitzva and make a zimun, for according to many they are obligated in zimun, and even according to those who disagree they have a mitzva in it. So too wrote the Ben Ish Ḥai, Koraḥ 13.
The Rishonim wrote that the reason women do not join with men for a zimun is "because of licentiousness" (Meiri, Ritva and Ran). The Ran explained (Megilla 6b, s.v. "matni'") that when their joining together creates a new reality of an obligation of zimun, there is an aspect of breaching the boundaries of modesty, because then they must unite together to create the obligation. According to this it is understood why, once there are three men and an obligation has been created, the women who sat there are also obligated to respond to their zimun (MB 17).
There is no impediment to women making a zimun in a place where there are men, and so wrote Halikhot Beita 12:7, based on Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach. And it seems that this is also implied by Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 199:6 and MB 18 (and not as Teshuvot Ve-hanhagot 4:51). And it is likewise understood that men answer a women's zimun, just as they answer "Amen" after a woman's blessings.
The law of joining a minor girl to two adult women is like the law of joining a minor boy to two adult men (below, halakha 9).

sections.body_en:
The Sages originally said that Torah scholars should not include amei ha-aretz (people ignorant of Torah) in a zimun, and this was a protest against the amei ha-aretz who did not study Torah and did not serve Torah scholars, so that it was not fitting for Torah scholars to join them at a meal. The intent was not, Heaven forbid, to cause a rift between Torah scholars and amei ha-aretz, for amei ha-aretz are counted in a minyan, and if they wish to study Torah, they should be taught willingly, and if they ask for help, it is a mitzva to do kindness with them. Rather, the closeness of hearts at a meal might blur the necessary protest against the amei ha-aretz. For the atmosphere at a meal is relaxed and open, and sometimes also includes drinking alcoholic beverages, and it is not fitting for Torah scholars to become so closely attached to a person who is not connected to Torah. Therefore, even if they ate together, and together with him they are three, since it is not fitting that they join together at a meal, they do not make a zimun including him (Berakhot 47b). However, the amei ha-aretz themselves, if three ate together, are obligated in zimun (Meiri; Ritva; BHL 199:3, s.v. "mezamnin alav").

However, afterward, in the days of the Rishonim, a ruling was issued that one should not distance the amei ha-aretz, for if they are distanced they will build an altar for themselves and distance themselves further from the path of Torah and mitzvot. Therefore, one should not distinguish between the law of zimun and the law of a minyan; and just as for a minyan of ten for prayer we include any Jew who wishes, even if he commits serious transgressions publicly, such as eating creeping creatures and pork, so we include any Jew who wishes to recite Birkat Ha-mazon in a zimun of three or ten. However, with one who commits transgressions out of spite, in order to defy the Torah and those who bear it, it is not fitting to sit at a meal, and consequently he should not be included in a zimun (SA 199:3).13

notes_en.en:
In Berakhot 47b the different views are explained as to who is the am ha-aretz who does not join the zimun, and Rav Huna said that the halakha follows "Aḥerim," that even one who did not serve Torah scholars is considered an am ha-aretz and does not join the zimun. And although for a minyan we include even a wicked person who commits transgressions, since the zimun is connected to a meal, it is not fitting that Torah scholars join to sit at one meal with amei ha-aretz who withhold themselves from Torah study and the observance of mitzvot, and consequently it is also not appropriate to include them in the zimun. Presumably the Sages wanted, through this protest, to arouse the amei ha-aretz to study Torah properly. However, afterward, in the period of the Rishonim, Tosafot (Ḥagiga 22a, and Berakhot there) wrote that we take into account the view of Rabbi Yose, who said regarding a similar matter that one should not distance amei ha-aretz and be stringent with them, so that they will not separate and make an altar for themselves. And so it was ruled in SA 199:3, that amei ha-aretz are included in the zimun. However, the Magen Avraham 199:2, MB 2 and BHL wrote that those who transgress publicly should not be included in the zimun. Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach and several other poskim of our time ruled that a secular Jew who is in the category of a "tinok she-nishba" (a "captured infant," one raised without knowledge of Torah) is included today in the zimun (Piskei Teshuvot 199:2; some disagree). However, all of the Magen Avraham's stringency regarding those who transgress publicly applies specifically when it concerned individuals, regarding whom there was no concern that they would distance themselves and build an altar for themselves, and only for the reason of "tinok she-nishba" were they lenient with them. But today, when unfortunately those who transgress publicly are numerous, and the concern is great that they will distance themselves as secular people or make an altar for themselves like the Reform, based on the reasoning of Rabbi Yose and Tosafot (and the Magen Avraham too agrees to this), one should rule in practice that anyone who wishes to join in fulfilling the mitzva of Birkat Ha-mazon is included in the zimun. It follows that in practice the law of zimun is like the law of inclusion in a minyan, and regarding a minyan they said that every Jew is included. Perhaps there is a certain distinction: regarding zimun, even with one who commits a single transgression out of spite, it is not fitting to sit at a meal, and consequently it is not fitting to include him in a zimun (like the original law of the am ha-aretz). But regarding a minyan, as long as he wishes to participate in mitzvot and wishes to pray, even though he has transgressions that he commits out of spite, perhaps he can be included in a minyan (see BHL 199:3; and see Peninei Halakha: Prayer 2:8). And see below 13:7 regarding sitting at a meal with amei ha-aretz.
One who eats non-kosher foods may not bless over his eating (see 12:10), and consequently he also does not join the zimun, as the Sages said in the Mishna (Berakhot 45a), that one who eats rabbinically untithed produce (tevel) does not join the zimun (SA 196:1).

sections.body_en:
The Rishonim and Aḥaronim disagree on the question of whether a minor joins the zimun (BY 199:10).

According to the custom of those of Ashkenazic descent, a minor is not included in the zimun, and only from the time a boy reaches the age of thirteen does he join the zimun (Rema 199:10).

According to the custom of those of Sephardic descent, one minor is included in the zimun, on condition that he understands to Whom one blesses and is at least six years old. Therefore, if two adults and a minor who understands to Whom one blesses ate together, one of the adults should lead the zimun. And if nine adults and a minor who understands to Whom one blesses ate together, the adult who leads the zimun mentions God's name (Rivash 451, as cited in BY; SA 199:10).14

notes_en.en:
The basis of the discussion is in Berakhot 47b and 48a, where views are cited as to when a minor is included in the zimun. At the end of the discussion they said that the halakha follows Rav Naḥman, who said: "A minor who knows to Whom one blesses – we make a zimun including him." So ruled the Rif, the Rambam, Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona and others, and so it was ruled in SA 199:10. In contrast, the view of Rav Natronai Gaon and Rav Sar Shalom Gaon, the Ravya, the Maharil and others is that a minor is not included in the zimun, and this is the Ashkenazic custom (Rema).
Although according to the Ashkenazic custom a minor is not included, if an Ashkenazi eats with a Sephardi who wishes to include a minor, the Ashkenazi may join them and complete for them a zimun of three. And if Sephardim wish to include an Ashkenazi in a zimun of ten with a minor, he should join them but not mention God's name, and the other participants in the zimun, who follow the Sephardic custom, should mention God's name (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach and Rav Eliyahu, as cited in Ve-zot Ha-berakha, p. 132. And see the Harḥavot regarding the minor's age).
A deaf person who can concentrate and respond to the zimun joins (Rema 199:10). A mute person who understands the zimun but cannot respond at all does not join according to the Ben Ish Ḥai, Koraḥ 12, and Arukh Ha-shulḥan 199:4, and joins according to Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 199:10. A deaf-mute who cannot speak at all and does not understand what is being discussed does not join according to all views (and see Peninei Halakha: Prayer 2:7, where it is explained that a completely mentally incompetent person does not join a minyan, and the same law applies to zimun). One drunk like Lot, who behaves like a completely incompetent person, does not join. A drunk person who cannot speak properly before the king joins for three but does not join for ten, and if he can speak before the king he joins for ten (MB 99:11). A sleeping person does not join for three, and for ten, in a pressing situation, one sleeping person is included, but not two (MB 55:33-34).

sections.title_en: Laws of Those Who Join the Zimun – With Which Food and When
sections.body_en:
If seven ate bread, and three ate with them a kezayit of fruit or vegetables, or even drank the measure of a revi'it of any beverage other than water, they join together for a zimun of ten, for they too are included in the call "of whose food we have eaten," and by virtue of them God's name is mentioned. But if only six ate bread, since there is no evident majority there who ate bread, they make a zimun without mentioning God's name (SA 197:2).15

Regarding a zimun of three, the Rishonim disagree. According to the Rambam, only if all three eat bread do they join together for a zimun. According to the Rif, even if two eat bread and the third eats mezonot, the third joins the zimun. And according to the Rosh, even if the third eats fruit or vegetables or a beverage other than water, he joins the zimun. In practice, if there were two who ate bread, ideally they should ask the third to eat bread with them, or at least foods of the mezonot type; and after the fact, even if he ate fruit or vegetables with them or drank a nourishing beverage, they should make a zimun with him (SA 197:3).

Those who join must be careful to recite the after-blessing after the zimun, and if they mistakenly blessed before the zimun, they can no longer join. The mezamen must be one of those who ate bread.16

Two who are eating together may include a third with them for a zimun as long as they have not made up their minds to finish their meal, and they are still in a state where, if a food they like very much were brought before them, they would eat some of it. For since they have not completely finished their meal, if a third person comes there and they are not in a hurry, it is a mitzva that they wait for him until he eats, so that they can bless with a zimun. And although in practice they will not eat with him, since they could have eaten with him, and they are waiting for him until he eats, they join together for a zimun (SA 197:1).17

notes_en.en: The poskim disagree on the question of what amount the one joining must eat. According to the Ra'ah and the Gra, there is no need to eat a kezayit or drink a revi'it in order to join the zimun. According to the Mordekhai and the Ravya, a kezayit or a revi'it is required, and so wrote SA 197:2 and most poskim. However, they disagree whether the measure of a kezayit and a revi'it is so that they will need to recite an after-blessing (Rashba), or because it is a significant amount (Pri Megadim). In practice, if there is an opinion that holds that an after-blessing should have been recited over the eating or drinking, for example if he drank most of a revi'it, or drank a hot beverage within the time of eating a peras, even though in practice one does not recite the blessing because of a doubt concerning blessings, the one who drank should be included in the zimun (see below 10:5; 10:10). And so it is implied by BHL. They likewise disagree about which beverage joins for a zimun: according to the Magen Avraham and others, even one who drinks water joins. But according to SA 197:2, most Aḥaronim and MB 12, one who drinks water does not join, but only one who drinks a nourishing beverage. The Aḥaronim of our time were in doubt regarding sweetened juice; see Ve-zot Ha-berakha p. 130. In practice it seems that one who drinks juice joins, since it has caloric value or other components such as vitamins and caffeine. So too wrote Arukh Ha-shulḥan 5, that anything that has some significance joins.

According to the Maharam, SA 197:3 and other Aḥaronim, the two should not suggest to the third that he eat vegetables or fruit or a beverage with them, so as not to enter into a doubt. According to many Aḥaronim, and so wrote the Knesset Ha-gedola and MB 22, if the third is not interested in eating mezonot, they should offer him fruit or vegetables or a beverage, in order to merit the zimun. When three ate bread and one mistakenly blessed, he joins with them for the zimun, as explained above in halakha 3. But when it concerns joining a third who ate mezonot or fruit, if one of them mistakenly recited the after-blessing or Birkat Ha-mazon, since he cut himself off from eating with them, they have lost the zimun (BHL 194:1, s.v. "eḥad"; MB 197:9).

If they wait for him until he finishes his eating, they are obligated to make a zimun. And if they wait until he eats a kezayit, they are permitted to make a zimun (and see above, note 2, item 4). The same law applies to seven who ate bread: if they wait for three to eat a kezayit of vegetables, they can make a zimun with them with the mention of God's name.

sections.title_en: One Who Needs to Leave Before the Zimun, Such as at a Wedding Meal
sections.body_en:
The obligation of the individual to stay with his companions until the zimun applies in an ordinary situation, but in a case of necessity or great need, it is permitted to withdraw from the group and bless without a zimun. For example, one who needs to leave in order to prevent financial loss to himself, or for the sake of a mitzva, may bless without a zimun. In such a situation, it is a custom of piety for his companions to join him for a zimun, and especially when they are two, it is proper that they join him for a zimun, for otherwise they will lose the mitzva of zimun.

This law is very common at wedding meals, for since they are very long, many find it difficult to stay until the end. Some will consequently find it difficult to get up the next day for prayer or will be tired at their work, and some are accustomed to set aside time every night for study, and if they stay until the end they will lose their fixed study. All these and the like are permitted to bless without a zimun. However, one who has no great need, since he joined in fellowship with everyone at the meal, is obligated to stay until the zimun and the Sheva Berakhot.

One who knows in advance that he will have to leave before the end of the meal should properly resolve in his mind that although he is dining with them, he is not fully joining them in fellowship, and preferably he should also tell his neighbors that he will have to leave before the end; in this way he will not become obligated in zimun and will be able to bless by himself even without great need. And if his tablemates wish to join him for a zimun, he should make a zimun with them, for since he in fact ate with them, even though he did not establish himself to eat together with them until the end, they may make a zimun with him.18

notes_en.en:
When the individual must leave, it is proper that they join him for a zimun, as cited in MB 200:5 and Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 7, that according to the Behag the two should act beyond the letter of the law. All the more so when without him they will have no zimun (see above, halakha 3 and note 4). The permission itself to leave for a great need is cited in BY 200:1. And it is implied from MB 200:5 and 193:16, 31 that the permission is specifically to prevent loss or for the sake of a mitzva that would be lost if he did not leave. The Yosef Ometz 159 wrote that losing a great deal of time, for one for whom this is difficult, also permits blessing without a zimun. Therefore at a wedding, even though the need to leave is not absolutely necessary, if it involves a great deal of time, one may be lenient even for an ordinary need. However, on the other hand one must remember that there is a mitzva to stay until the end of the wedding meal, and it is cited in the name of Rav Ḥayim of Brisk that the words of Ḥazal (Berakhot 6b), "Whoever derives benefit from a bridegroom's meal and does not gladden him transgresses the five voices," are directed toward one who does not wait until the Sheva Berakhot. Therefore one should not be lenient in this without a real need. And one who knows that he will have to leave should resolve in his mind from the outset that he is not joining them in fellowship at the meal, and in this way he will not become obligated in zimun (Igrot Moshe OḤ 1:56, based on Rema 193:3). Some suggested that one who intends to leave before the end should make sure to begin the meal after his companions have eaten a kezayit of bread, for then according to Tosafot (45a) he is not considered as joining them in fellowship (Birkat Hashem vol. 2, 6:12). It is better that he tell them that he will have to leave before the end, for in this way he does not join them in fellowship (Igrot Moshe there).
Whoever is permitted to withdraw from the zimun is permitted to withdraw before the Sheva Berakhot, for the obligation of them is no greater than the obligation of zimun (see Otzar Ha-poskim 62:25:10). And if there are two there who are willing to join him for a zimun, he should make a zimun quietly with three. It seems that if they are at a wedding, they should say "she-ha-simḥa bi-m'ono" ("in whose abode is joy"). But they should not recite "Asher Bara," since it requires a cup, and if they make a zimun over a cup of wine, it may offend the groom. It is good that those who join the zimun afterward eat another kezayit, so that they will be true participants in the zimun of ten (see MB 200, end of se'if katan 9, and as cited in the next halakha). In any case, even if they afterward ate a kezayit of bread, they cannot be the ones leading the zimun, but they can recite Sheva Berakhot.
If there are ten there who want to bless, they should not make a zimun with ten, because this offends the groom, that an entire group withdraws in the middle of the meal (see SA 193:1). But if it concerns distinguished people such as rabbis whose time is precious, and the groom wants them to make a zimun with ten, or the groom knows that the meal is long and agrees that they withdraw in the middle, it is proper that those leaving make a zimun with ten over a cup of wine and recite Sheva Berakhot. And if it is difficult for them to gather ten, they should make a zimun with three over the cup and recite "Asher Bara." In any case, at the end of the meal the remaining diners should make a zimun and recite Sheva Berakhot again. We find something similar in what SA EH 62:11 wrote, that it is possible that at a wedding meal there will be several groups that recite Sheva Berakhot. And it is evident from the SA there that there is no need for the groom to sit with them, for one may recite Sheva Berakhot at a groom's meal even when he does not hear the blessings, and so wrote Arukh Ha-shulḥan 62:37.

sections.title_en: Whether One Who Participated in a Zimun Can Join Another Zimun
sections.body_en:
Three who ate together, and one of them wanted to bless and leave, and his companions agreed to join him for a zimun: if afterward another person comes and eats together with them and wants to make a zimun, they may not make a zimun with him, for they have already fulfilled the obligation of zimun, and it is not possible to make a zimun twice at one meal.

But if one person joined his companions who wanted to leave and answered the zimun with them, and afterward two more came and ate with him, he joins them for a zimun. For since there are two there who have not fulfilled the obligation of zimun, they can include the third who ate with them in the zimun. But he himself cannot be the mezamen, since he has already fulfilled the obligation of zimun. And so that person who has already fulfilled the obligation of zimun can complete a zimun for another two, and afterward for another two, without limit. For as long as there are two there who have not yet fulfilled the obligation of zimun, and he eats a kezayit with them, even though he has already fulfilled the zimun, he can join an additional zimun (MB 200:9).19

When ten ate together, and some of them finished their meal and asked those continuing to eat to join them for a zimun with the mention of God's name: as we have learned (halakha 3), if those finishing are the majority, the minority must join them. And if those finishing are a minority, the rest are not obligated to join them, but it is a custom of piety that they join. In any case, when those who are still in the middle of their meal join the zimun of ten and continue eating, they can make a zimun for themselves at the end of their meal without mentioning God's name, for since they joined the ten so that they could mention God's name, they did not lose the right to make a zimun for themselves adjacent to Birkat Ha-mazon. And even if those remaining were ten, they should not make a zimun with the mention of God's name, because they have already fulfilled the mitzva of mentioning God's name in the zimun, and it is not possible to fulfill this mitzva twice at the same meal.

And if five who have not yet made any zimun joined there, and together with those who already answered the zimun with the mention of God's name they are ten, and they ate another kezayit together, those five new ones have a mitzva to make a zimun with the mention of God's name. And although they are not the majority of the quorum, regarding the mention of God's name in the zimun a majority is not required; it suffices that they not be a minority. Provided that one of the five new ones leads the zimun (MB 200:9).20

notes_en.en: They must eat a kezayit of bread with him, and it suffices for him to eat a kezayit of vegetables or drink a nourishing beverage, as explained above in halakha 10. They further disagreed on this matter regarding a group of five, one of whom joined two of them for a zimun: according to the Magen Avraham, the Ḥayei Adam and MB 200:9, that one cannot afterward join the other two, for since they are one group that may not split up, if three of them made a zimun, the remaining two have lost their mitzva. But according to the Even Ha-ozer, Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 200:2, Arukh Ha-shulḥan 5 and Tehilla Le-David 1, that one can complete a zimun for the remaining two. And this is the halakha, as we have learned (note 2) that in a case of doubtful zimun, one makes a zimun.

If those who already made a zimun are three, they can make a zimun with ten if the seven ate a kezayit of bread, and the three who already made a zimun eat with them a kezayit of vegetables or the like. And if there are four or five there who have already fulfilled the zimun, they join only if they all eat a kezayit of bread together (MB 200:9).

sections.body_en:
The Sages instituted reciting Birkat Ha-mazon over a cup of wine, so that it will be said with festiveness and joy, and this cup is called the "kos shel berakha" ("cup of blessing"). What is special about wine is that it both nourishes and gladdens. When we bless God over a cup of wine, we thereby show that the blessing is complete: we thank God both for the food He has given us and for the Divine content that grants meaning and joy to our lives. Indeed, in Birkat Ha-mazon we express the Divine content of our existence in this world: to reveal the Shekhina in the good land that He has given us, through the covenant and the Torah, Jerusalem, the kingship of Israel and the Temple. Some do not grasp this matter and relate to Birkat Ha-mazon as a burden imposed on a person, that after he has enjoyed himself he must pay a "tax" – a blessing to God. But the truth is that Birkat Ha-mazon is the high point of the entire meal. For by being satisfied and even enjoying the food, we can reach the elevated level at which we thank and bless God. And when we do this over a cup of wine, the spiritual joy expressed in Birkat Ha-mazon is revealed in physical joy as well, for after we have merited to bless God, we drink of the wine and rejoice before God.

The Sages said (Berakhot 51a): "Whoever blesses over a full cup is given an inheritance without bounds," and "he merits and inherits two worlds, this world and the World to Come." By combining the Divine content of Birkat Ha-mazon with the joy and enjoyment of this world, the Divine blessing is revealed in completeness, in this world and in the World to Come. And since it is a Divine blessing, it has no limits; even when it is revealed in this limited world, it spreads out without bounds.

The poskim disagree on the question of in which situation it is fitting to bless over a cup of wine. Some say that even an individual must bless over a cup of wine, and if he has no wine and expects to have wine in a few more hours, he should not eat bread in the meantime, so that he will not recite Birkat Ha-mazon without a cup of wine. And if two are eating, each one must bless over a cup of wine, and if they are three, one cup suffices for them, over which the mezamen blesses (Rosh and Tur).

And some say that only when they are obligated in a zimun of three or ten is their Birkat Ha-mazon important and requires a cup of wine, but when they do not make a zimun, they do not bless over a cup (Hagahot Maimoniyot in the name of the Ri). And some say that even if they make a zimun with ten, they are not obligated to bless over a cup, but it is the choicest way of fulfilling the mitzva (mitzva min ha-muvḥar) (Rif and Rambam).

In practice, when there is no zimun, it is not customary to bless over a cup of wine (MB 182:16). And when blessing with a zimun, it is a mitzva to bless over a cup of wine, but it is not an obligation. Therefore, even those who are accustomed to enhance their observance of mitzvot, when it is difficult for them to obtain wine or difficult for them to drink wine, or they do not want to take the trouble, do not make the zimun over a cup. On Shabbat and Yom Tov it is customary to be more meticulous about this. And at important celebrations, when making a zimun with ten, it is customary to be careful to make the zimun over a cup.21

notes_en.en: SA 182:1 mentioned the three views in the order in which I have written them, and according to the rules of halakha, the view of the last "some say" is the main halakhic view. This is also the view of most Aḥaronim, that the blessing over the cup is not an obligation but a mitzva, and this is the custom, as MB 4 wrote. In the plain sense, those who wish to enhance the mitzva should bless over a cup of wine even as individuals; however, according to the Zohar and the Arizal, one does not bless over a cup of wine without a zimun, and this is the custom (MB 15-16; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 1). On Shabbat and Yom Tov people are more meticulous to make the zimun over a cup, as explained in the Shela and Arukh Ha-shulḥan 182:1.

sections.title_en: Laws of the Cup of Blessing
sections.body_en:
The Sages instituted several blessings to be said over a cup of wine: Birkat Ha-mazon, the blessings of betrothal and marriage, and Kiddush. Wherever the Sages instituted blessing over a cup, the intent is a cup that holds at least the measure of a revi'it of a log of wine (75 ml; Shabbat 76b; below 10:10).

The cup must be whole, without a defect or break in its rim or base. When there is no whole cup there, one may after the fact make Kiddush over a cup that has a defect. But if it has a crack through which the wine leaks, so that it does not hold a revi'it of wine, it is invalid (SA 183:3; MB 11; Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 14).

It is fitting to choose a beautiful cup for the blessing. When there is no cup there other than a simple disposable cup, one may bless over it after the fact (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 6:6, note 7).

One must be careful that the cup be completely clean, and if people drank from it or it became dirty in another way, it should be prepared for the blessing by rinsing it on the inside and washing it on the outside (SA 183:1). After the fact, when it is difficult to wash the cup, one may wipe it and clean it with a napkin (MB 1).

Although according to the law a cup holding only the measure of a revi'it suffices, if the cup holds more than the measure of a revi'it, it is a mitzva to fill it with wine, for such is the honor of the blessing, that it be said over a cup that has been filled abundantly. Some are accustomed to be meticulous to fill the cup to the brim, so that it is likely that during the blessing some wine will spill on the hand of the one blessing. But it seems that it is more of an enhancement to fill the cup until close to its rim, so that wine will not spill on the hand of the one blessing, and this is what the Sages meant when they said "a full cup" (Taz 183:4; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 4; MB 183:9. And so it is evident from the Gemara in Berakhot 52b, from the explanation of the words of Beit Hillel).

The Sages said that one must dilute the wine with water so that it will be pleasant to drink, for in their time the wine was undiluted, and without diluting it with water its taste was too strong (Berakhot 50b). And they said to complete its dilution at the blessing of the land, in order to show thereby the praise of the land, whose wines are strong (Berakhot 51a). But today, when one buys ready-made wine, there is no need to dilute it, for even before it was put into the bottle it was flavored in the finest manner (Rema 183:2). Those who conduct themselves according to Kabbala are nevertheless accustomed to dilute the wine with a little water at the blessing of the land (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 6).

One must pour the wine from the bottle for the sake of the mitzva of the cup of blessing, and it is good to do this close to the blessing (Rema 183:2; Magen Avraham 3).

The Sages said (Berakhot 51a) that one should first take the cup in both hands, in order thereby to express his fondness for it, and afterward, when he leads the zimun and blesses, he should hold it in his right hand alone, which is the important hand. He should hold the cup with all his fingers, so that the fingers will crown the cup. He should raise the cup a handbreadth above the table, so that it will be seen by all. He should set his eyes on the cup, so that he will not divert his attention. If he needs to, he may look in the siddur, and it is good to bring the siddur close to the cup so that he will see both. After he drinks from the wine, it is good that he send the cup to his wife, so that she too will drink from the wine, for in this way the blessing will spread to her and to him (as explained in the next section).22

notes_en.en:
Berakhot 51a: "Ten things were said regarding the cup of blessing: it requires rinsing and washing; undiluted (ḥai), and full; crowning, and wrapping; he takes it in both hands, and places it in the right; he raises it a handbreadth from the ground, and sets his eyes on it; and some say: he also sends it as a gift to the members of his household. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: We have only four: rinsing, washing, undiluted, and full." The Rambam mentioned only the four things that Rabbi Yoḥanan said. However, this is difficult, for Rabbi Yoḥanan himself raises the question of whether the left hand may assist the right. Indeed, the Geonim wrote that all ten are halakha. The Rosh wrote that only crowning and wrapping are not halakha. According to Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, five are halakha: the first four and also placing it in the right hand, and the rest are not obligatory. The Gra (183:7) explained that the four things are indispensable and the rest are for the sake of the mitzva.
They disagreed about the meaning of "ḥai" (which is one of the four things that are practiced according to all views), and in practice all the interpretations were ruled as halakha. Some explained that the cup should be whole (Tosafot; SA 183:3). Some explained that in times when they had undiluted ("ḥai") wine, that is, not diluted with water, one should pour the undiluted wine into the cup, and only afterward dilute it with water, as the Sages said (Berakhot 50b); and they further said that one should dilute it at the blessing of the land (ibid. 51a). According to Rabbeinu Tam the meaning is that one should finish diluting at the blessing of the land, but one may begin before Birkat Ha-mazon; and according to the Rif, one should dilute it with water only at the blessing of the land (see BY 183:2). And some explained that one should pour the wine from the bottle into the cup in honor of the blessing (Rashi; Rema 183:2; MB 8).
A left-handed person, according to MB 183:20, should take the cup in his left hand, which is the strong one for him. The Kabbalists and some of the poskim wrote that every person should hold it in the right hand, and so many are accustomed (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 183:29; Piskei Teshuvot 183:13).
As we have learned, the two enhancements that people are less careful about are "crowning and wrapping." They disagreed in the Gemara (Berakhot 51a) about what crowning is: according to Rav Yehuda, he crowns it with students who stand around him during the blessing; according to Rav Ḥisda, he crowns it with fine cups. See MB 183:15, Kaf Ha-ḥayim 20 and Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 6, note 9, regarding the different views on how one should properly hold the cup with the fingers. Perhaps it can be said that by holding the cup with all the fingers there is crowning. And in whatever way one takes the cup with all his fingers, he acts properly according to one of the views, and so I wrote above. Some said that by not filling the cup completely one fulfills the crowning, for what remains at the top of the cup is like a crown (however, the Taz 4 and Magen Avraham 4 rejected their reasoning). Wrapping: according to the Beit Yosef, the enhancement is that one wrap himself in a tallit. Today, for those who always go about in a hat and jacket, he should wrap himself in them (MB 183:11), as I wrote above 4:12. And some say that the very fact that one covers his head with a kippa and covers his body as in prayer means that he fulfills wrapping (Rabbeinu Yeruḥam; Darkhei Moshe 183:1). Indeed, ideally those eating at the beach or the pool should recite Birkat Ha-mazon when dressed in a shirt and trousers, as in prayer (see Peninei Halakha: Prayer 5:4-5).
When wine is expensive and hard to obtain, in many places it was customary to bless over "ḥamar medina" (a "national beverage"), that is, an important beverage with which guests are customarily honored (Rema 182:2). According to many, it must contain alcohol (see Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 8:4). According to Tehilla Le-David 182:2, one who prefers "ḥamar medina" may bless over it even when there is wine there. According to Kabbala one should bless specifically over wine (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 182:14).

sections.body_en:
After finishing Birkat Ha-mazon, the mezamen recites "Borei Pri Ha-gafen" and drinks from the wine. According to the law, in order to fulfill the mitzva of drinking from the cup of blessing, it suffices that the mezamen drink the measure of "melo lugmav" (a cheekful), which for an average person is about 50 ml (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 6:5). However, since he did not drink a revi'it, he has lost the after-blessing over the wine; therefore it is good that he drink a revi'it (75 ml) and recite Me'ein Shalosh after drinking (see SA 190:3).

If the mezamen finds it difficult to drink the measure of melo lugmav from the wine, the mezamen may bless and taste a little of the wine, and one of the diners should drink the measure of melo lugmav in his place (SA OḤ 190:4). And if several of the diners together drink the measure of melo lugmav, they have fulfilled the mitzva after the fact (SA OḤ 271:14; MB 73; Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 6:5, note 6).

Although in terms of the mitzva it suffices that one of the diners drink the measure of melo lugmav from the cup, the choicest way of fulfilling the mitzva is that everyone drink from the wine, as is customary at Kiddush, so that everyone will be partners in the cup of blessing. It is especially fitting for a person to send the cup over which he blessed to his wife, for there is a segula in this, that through it the blessing will be drawn to her and to him (Berakhot 51b; SA 183:4).23

As with Kiddush, so too with the cup of blessing one must be careful that the wine not be pagum ("defective"). Pagum wine is wine from which someone has already drunk. The wine is considered pagum only for a new drinking; for example, if one drank from the Kiddush cup on Friday night, the wine remaining in the cup is considered pagum for the Kiddush of Shabbat day.
