But on Friday night, the listeners may drink from the Kiddush cup even though the one making Kiddush has already drunk from it, because their drinking is considered a continuation of his drinking, and the wine in the cup is not considered pagum with respect to them throughout the drinking of that same mitzva. And so many are accustomed, that the wife drinks from her husband's cup of blessing and of Kiddush. However, regarding the other diners, especially those who are not close family members, this is not proper etiquette (derekh eretz), for many do not want to drink from another person's cup. And so it was ruled in halakha, that a person should not pass the cup from which he drank to his fellow, lest he find it repulsive and be embarrassed to tell him so. Furthermore, perhaps the one who drank first is ill, and the second, who drinks from his cup, will catch his illness (SA OḤ 170:16; MB 37; and below 12:5).

Therefore it is preferred that the one blessing pour from his cup into the other cups; but then their drinking is not a direct continuation of his drinking, and since he has already drunk from the wine, the wine he pours into their cups is considered pagum and is not fit for the cup of blessing. The solution to this is that after the mezamen recites the blessing over the vine, and before he begins to drink, he should pour from the cup of blessing into another cup and drink from it; in this way the wine that remains in the cup of blessing will not become pagum, and he will be able to pour from it into the cups of the other diners. And if the wine in the cup is not enough for all who want to drink, he should add more wine from the bottle to the wine in the cup and pour into their cups.

The most enhanced way is that even before Birkat Ha-mazon, wine be poured into the cups of all the diners who wish to taste the wine of the blessing. There is no need to wash their cups first, nor is there a need for each one to have the measure of a revi'it of wine in his cup; rather, they should pour according to what they want to drink after the blessing, for the main cup of blessing is the cup of the one blessing, and only regarding it must one be careful that it be clean and contain the measure of a revi'it. After the one blessing finishes Birkat Ha-mazon, he should recite the blessing over the wine, and everyone should answer "Amen" and drink from the cups before them. This way is considered the most enhanced, because there is no interruption at all in it between hearing the blessing of Ha-gafen and drinking the wine, and the wine they drink has not become pagum at all through the drinking of the one blessing. However, many are not so exacting about the laws of etiquette, and they give the other diners from the cup from which the one blessing drank; whoever is not repelled by this drinks, and the others, who are repelled by it, do not drink. But as stated, the most enhanced way, both in Birkat Ha-mazon and in Kiddush, is to make sure that there is no defect or trace of repulsiveness in the wine of the cup of blessing, so that everyone will be able to enhance the mitzva and drink from the wine.24

It is important to note that the diners fulfill their obligation with the mezamen's blessing over the wine only if they intended to fulfill their obligation. But if they thought that wine would not be poured for them, and in the end the cup was brought to them or wine was poured for them, they must recite "Borei Pri Ha-gafen" before they drink (SA 190:5).

notes_en.en: Since the wife is blessed, the husband in turn is blessed as well, for they said (Bava Metzia 59a): "Blessing is found in a man's home only on account of his wife." And they said (Yevamot 62b): "Any man who has no wife dwells without blessing."

In Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 190:5 the matters are explained at length. The details of the law of the cup of blessing, that it not be pagum, how it can be remedied, and that in a pressing situation one may bless over a pagum cup, are explained in SA 182:3-7; SA 271:16-17; Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 6:6-7 and note 8. See further there, note 10, regarding the law of speaking between the blessing over the wine and the drinking, for the listeners who want to drink from the cup of blessing.
One may raise a difficulty regarding the custom of many who drink from the cup of blessing and are not concerned about catching an illness (see SA 170:16; MB 37). Indeed, the Ben Ish Ḥai (Be-har 13) wrote that people drink only when they know that the one who drank before them is not ill. And some wrote that perhaps the merit of the mitzva protects (Sdei Ḥemed).
